name: C#
title: C# (13)

preamble.text: Analysis against C# 13 (.NET 9). C# 12/13 add primary constructors, collection expressions, params collections, and lock type.

type.text: **Interfaces + extension methods**: Can add behavior without coupling to classes
**Generics with constraints**: Better than Java (no erasure, value type generics)
**LINQ separates iteration from logic**: Query syntax decouples data operations
**Inheritance still available**: Can couple via class hierarchies
**Nullable reference types (C# 8+)**: Separates nullable from non-nullable
**File-scoped types (C# 11)**: `file` access modifier restricts visibility to a source file, tightening encapsulation
**Null still exists alongside nullable types**: Migration incomplete
**Properties can have side effects**: `obj.Prop` might do anything
**.NET runtime allows reflection**: Can break encapsulation
Char is documented as a UTF-16 code unit; String.Length counts units

construction.text: **Records (C# 9+) are immutable**: Value semantics prevent coupling
**Primary constructors (C# 12)**: Reduce construction boilerplate on class/struct
**Collection expressions (C# 12)**: `[1, 2, 3]` unified syntax decouples creation from collection type
**Constructors can have side effects**: No enforcement of pure construction
**DI built into ASP.NET Core**: Framework-level construction decoupling
**Collection order is unpinned**: the documentation warns that Dictionary iteration order must not be relied on, and the ordered collections are opt-in

**One value, many names**: class instances move by reference, a field, a parameter, and a lambda share one object, and no declaration names the alias set (readonly is a discipline on the field, not the graph)
**Execution moves with no call in sight**: user-defined implicit conversion operators run at assignment and argument sites
ECMA-335 declares the order in which static constructors run unpredictable

memory.text: **.NET GC decouples memory**: Generational GC (gen0, gen1, gen2, LOH)
**No manual memory management for managed code**: Safe by default
**GC pauses affect latency**: Server/workstation GC modes, background GC helps
**IDisposable pattern for resources**: Deterministic cleanup via `using` statement
**Finalizers couple cleanup to GC**: Non-deterministic timing
**Stack-allocated structs**: Value types avoid GC but couple to stack lifetime
**Span<T> reduces allocations**: Stack-based memory without GC pressure
**The class is declared**: OutOfMemoryException carries a documented contract (the runtime restores the process after a heap failure) and is catchable

error.text: **Result types uncommon**: Libraries exist (LanguageExt) but not idiomatic
**Nullable pattern helps**: `?.` operator reduces null coupling
**A fault ends the process**: an unhandled exception in any thread terminates the process (documented); try/catch recovers in the frame, and no unit is declared

concurrency.text: **Async/await excellent**: Best async syntax in mainstream languages
**Task<T> separates async**: Clear distinction from sync code
**Lock type (C# 13)**: Dedicated `System.Threading.Lock` with pattern-based `using` scoping — decouples synchronization from `object` casting
**Can still use threads with shared state**: Traditional coupling available
**Immutable collections available**: System.Collections.Immutable, FrozenSet/FrozenDictionary (C# 12+) prevent concurrent coupling with zero overhead

platform.text: **Open-source runtime and compiler**: .NET is MIT licensed, and the Roslyn compiler is developed in the open
**Cross-platform runtime**: The same compiled library runs on Windows, Linux, macOS, Android, iOS, and WebAssembly (Blazor)
**Multiple implementations**: CoreCLR, Mono, and .NET Framework each run C# code, so the language is not bound to one runtime
**No runtime version lock-in**: Side-by-side runtime versions let an application pin its own .NET version

performance.text: **Excellent JIT optimization**: CLR is highly optimized
**GC pauses**: Server and background modes bound the pause but do not remove it, and the collector decides when it runs
**Tunable GC**: Multiple GC modes for different scenarios
**Span<T>/Memory<T>**: Zero-copy optimizations decouple performance from allocations
**Native AOT**: Recent addition decouples from JIT

ecosystem.text: **Framework monoculture**: ASP.NET Core and the Microsoft stack dominate, so the alternatives are not really alternatives
**CLR metadata carries a published promise**: IL assemblies follow a standardised format, and the runtime publishes its compatibility rules [@ecma335; @dotnetCompat]

**Stored payloads bind to the runtime**: Microsoft states that BinaryFormatter throws NotSupportedException across nearly all project types from .NET 8, and that .NET 9 removed the in-box implementation and the settings that enabled it, so a payload written on an older runtime no longer has a reader [@netBinFmtDisabled; @netBinFmtRemoved]

evolution.text: **Build variants multiply**: #if blocks with DefineConstants select which members compile, and the flag set lives in the project file, not the source

domain.text: **Web frontend**: Blazor exists but less common

learning.text: **Many features**: LINQ, async, delegates can overwhelm

syntax.text: **Less verbose than Java**: Properties, expression bodies
**Type inference limited**: Often need explicit types
**Modern features**: Pattern matching, records reduce boilerplate

testing.text: **World-class debugger**: Visual Studio debugger is best-in-class

security.text: **Nullable reference types**: Eliminates many null bugs
The default unchecked arithmetic wraps Int32/Int64 in two's complement; `checked` is the opt-in, a mitigation

tradeoffs: **`async` colours a method**: The modifier changes what its callers must do, so synchronous and asynchronous code do not compose freely — a deliberate trade
**Nullability checking is a project setting**: `<Nullable>enable</Nullable>` turns the checks on per project, so adoption is incremental — a migration choice, not a forced dependency
**Unsafe code stays in the language**: Pointers, P/Invoke, and COM are available for what the managed runtime cannot serve, a deliberate escape hatch rather than a dependency
**Two runtimes share the language**: Code that must also run on .NET Framework limits itself to the common subset — a compatibility trade, not a coupling
**Code generation is part of the build**: Source generators and `partial` types let tooling contribute half of a class, which moves work into the compilation step
verdict: C# has evolved strong coupling-reducing features (extension methods, LINQ, records, async/await, nullable types) while maintaining .NET compatibility. Better than Java for coupling reduction due to modern features. Main strength: async/await eliminates coupling in this dimension. Main weakness: unchecked exceptions hide failure coupling.

energy.text: Runs on a virtual machine, above native code in the energy and time benchmarks [@pereira2017energy]; a causal re-analysis attributes most of the gap to execution time [@vankempen2025green].

ai-readiness.text: A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [@joel2025lowresource; @effibenchx2025].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

delivery.note: IL and assembly metadata follow a published standard, and the runtime publishes its compatibility rules

data_formats.note: Microsoft states that BinaryFormatter.Serialize and BinaryFormatter.Deserialize throw NotSupportedException at runtime across nearly all project types starting in .NET 8, and that in .NET 9 the in-box implementation throws on use even with the settings that previously enabled it, because those settings are removed
